claim.pdf_says: BINARY-CHAR UNSIGNED 0 £ n < 256 [2**8] / BINARY-SHORT UNSIGNED 0 £ n < 65536 [2**16] / BINARY-LONG UNSIGNED 0 £ n < 4294967296 [2**32] / BINARY-DOUBLE UNSIGNED 0 £ n < 2**64  (the '£' is the glyph the ISO PDF itself paints: a Symbol-font 'less-than-or-equal' at code point 0xA3 emitted under a text-font encoding, so it images as a pound sign)
claim.markdown_says:
| BINARY-CHAR UNSIGNED | 0 | £ n < | 256 [2\*\*8] |
| BINARY-SHORT UNSIGNED | 0 | £ n < | 65536 [2\*\*16] |
| BINARY-LONG UNSIGNED | 0 | £ n < | 4294967296 [2\*\*32] |
| BINARY-DOUBLE UNSIGNED | 0 | £ n < | 2\*\*64 |
claim.why_it_matters: NOT a transcription slip - the markdown faithfully copies the broken glyph the PDF prints, so a verifier re-reading page 537 will see '£' in both. The defect is inherited from ISO's own PDF font encoding, and it destroys normative content: 13.18.60.4 General rule 12 defines the minimum range each binary-N usage must represent, and the left-hand operator is what says whether the lower bound is inclusive. Read literally, '0 £ n < 256' has no meaning; the intended relation on every UNSIGNED row is '0 <= n < 2**8' etc. (the SIGNED rows correctly show '<' because -128 is excluded, and an unsigned item must be able to hold 0, so the unsigned operator can only be '<='). The same mis-mapped 0xA3 will recur wherever the standard prints a less-than-or-equal, so this is a pattern to sweep, not a one-off.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED as a PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy - there is no discrepancy at all, and the claim concedes this in its own words ('NOT a transcription slip - the markdown faithfully copies the broken glyph the PDF prints').

What I independently verified, at 300 dpi and 3x upscale on the operator column of the GR-12 minimum-range table (E:/Temp/specrecon/v537/spec_p537.png, crop E:/Temp/specrecon/v537/crop_ops.png):

1. THE PRINTED GLYPHS. Reading the glyphs myself, row by row: the four SIGNED rows (BINARY-CHAR/-SHORT/-LONG/-DOUBLE SIGNED) each paint a plain less-than '<' in the left operator slot. The four UNSIGNED rows each paint an unmistakable pound sign '£' - top loop, descending vertical, horizontal crossbar, bottom foot stroke. It is not a degraded '<=' and not a '≤'; the ISO PDF really images a pound sign.

2. BOTH QUOTES ARE ACCURATE, AND THE TWO SOURCES AGREE. specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 22537, 22539, 22541, 22543 read exactly '| BINARY-CHAR UNSIGNED | 0 | £ n < | 256 [2\*\*8] |' and siblings - character-for-character what the PDF prints. The markdown is a faithful transcription. Nothing was lost, reflowed, dropped, or mis-OCR'd. The reconciliation ledger's job is PDF-vs-markdown fidelity, and on this point fidelity is perfect. Editing the markdown to '<=' would make the transcription DIVERGE from its canonical source - the opposite of reconciliation. Classifying this 'ocr-error' is therefore wrong on its face.

3. THE 'PATTERN TO SWEEP' CLAIM IS EMPIRICALLY FALSE. A repo-wide grep of specs/ISO_COBOL.md returns exactly 4 occurrences of '£' in the entire ~1000-page transcription - all 4 are the rows on this one page - and ZERO occurrences of '≤'. There is no recurring mis-mapping to sweep; it is a one-off confined to this single table.

4. THE STATED ETIOLOGY IS UNSUPPORTED. The claim asserts 'a Symbol-font less-than-or-equal at code point 0xA3 emitted under a text-font encoding'. Page 537 carries no Symbol font: its font dictionary is only MLLGKI+Cambria,Bold (Type0/Identity-H), MLLGNI+Cambria (Type0/Identity-H), and ArialNarrow (TrueType/WinAnsiEncoding). In the obfuscated Identity-H text layer the SIGNED operator is CID U+03B4 and the UNSIGNED operator is CID U+0349 - two distinct subset CIDs, neither of which is 0xA3. So the specific mechanism cited is invented, not observed.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE, AND WHERE IT BELONGS. The substantive semantic observation stands on its own merits and I do not dispute it: '0 £ n < 256' is not a readable relation, and the only coherent reading of the UNSIGNED rows is '0 <= n < 2**8' (etc.), because an unsigned item must be able to represent 0. The SIGNED rows' '<' is genuinely intentional rather than a second defect - '-128 [-2**7] < n < 128 [2**7]' states a minimum range of -127..127 precisely so that one's-complement and sign-magnitude representations satisfy it, so no correction is warranted there. But this is a DEFECT IN ISO'S OWN PUBLISHED PDF, not a discrepancy between the PDF and its transcription. It belongs in an ISO-defect register (per the project's practice of recording ISO's own defects), annotated in place with an editorial note, and NOT in the spec-reconciliation ledger as a transcription fix.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a reconciliation finding. The PDF and specs/ISO_COBOL.md agree character-for-character: both print '£' as the left-hand operator on the four UNSIGNED rows of the 13.18.60.4 GR-12 minimum-range table, and both print '<' on the four SIGNED rows. The transcription is faithful, so there is nothing to reconcile and the 'ocr-error' classification is incorrect. Two supporting assertions in the claim are also wrong: (a) it is NOT a recurring pattern - '£' appears exactly 4 times in the whole markdown, all on this page, and '≤' appears 0 times; (b) the Symbol-font-0xA3 etiology is unsupported - page 537 uses only Cambria (Identity-H subsets) and ArialNarrow, with obfuscated CIDs U+03B4 ('<') and U+0349 ('£'). The one true kernel is a defect in ISO's published PDF: '0 £ n < 256' is unreadable and the intended relation is '0 <= n < 2**8' (the SIGNED rows' '<' is correct as printed, since '-128 < n < 128' deliberately states a -127..127 minimum so one's-complement and sign-magnitude machines conform). Record that in the ISO-defect register with an in-place editorial note; do not alter the transcription, which would break its fidelity to the canonical source.
